label: Asks two things at once
why: A respondent happy with one service and unhappy with the other has no true answer. A single rating mixes two objects.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Respondents may think of kerb collection, drop-off sites or bins differently. The brief does not say which is meant.

label: No route for no opinion
why: Respondents who do not use a service or cannot judge it have no clear option, so they may pick the midpoint.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Respondents may think of income, savings, debts or spending, and of themselves or their household. Each reads the phrase differently, so answers are not comparable.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: The ends differ in kind and strength: "comfortably" has no intensity word, while "very difficult" does. The in-between options were not shown, so balance cannot be fully checked.

label: Respondent must add up
quote: vigorous physical activity and moderate physical activity combined
why: Respondents must work out hours for two kinds of activity and add them in their head. Two different things are asked at once.

label: Words with more than one meaning
quote: vigorous physical activity and moderate physical activity
why: Respondents will draw the line between vigorous and moderate differently. It is also unclear whether work, housework or walking count.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: 'Typical' has no clear start or end. Respondents must average over varying weeks, so each person builds the answer differently.

label: Amount asked with vague categories
why: Categories are not shown, so fit cannot be judged. Respondents read the scale as what is normal; the top may be too low or too high.

label: Pushes toward one answer
quote: Given the growing pressure on public services
why: States a contested claim as fact and pushes respondents toward agreeing with reduction before they judge the issue themselves.

label: Negation in the question
why: Negative, leading question form combined with agree-disagree options; it is unclear whether agreeing means yes or no to the idea.

label: Asks two things at once
quote: particularly those who may not contribute to the economy
why: Adds a second target: all immigrants versus only some. A respondent who wants fewer of one group but not the other cannot answer.

label: Stem states only one side
quote: should do more to reduce the number of immigrants
why: Only the reduction position is stated. Respondents who want the number kept or increased are not offered their view in the stem.

label: Agree-disagree instead of construct's terms
why: The statement holds a quantity and a direction, so agree-disagree adds acquiescence risk and makes respondents answer two things at once.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Vague: it could mean tougher laws, tighter borders or something else. 'Immigrants' and 'may not contribute' also have open boundaries.

label: No route for no opinion
why: No don't-know option is shown, so respondents with no view may be pushed to invent one. Confirm one is offered.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
why: Adults who are unemployed, retired, studying or not in paid work have no terms of employment to rate and cannot answer truthfully.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Some will think of pay, others of hours, contract type or leave. The phrase does not say what counts, so people rate different things.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
quote: Completely satisfied / Very satisfied / Fairly satisfied / Not very satisfied / Not at all satisfied
why: Three positive points against two negative ones, with no middle option and no 'dissatisfied' wording. Neutral or mildly unhappy people have no matching answer.

label: Words with more than one meaning
quote: your household's total monthly income from all sources
why: It does not say who counts as the household or which money counts as income (pay, benefits, pensions, gifts, savings interest).

label: Hard recall or mental arithmetic
quote: total monthly income from all sources
why: Respondent must add several people's money from several sources, and convert weekly or yearly pay to a month. Others' income may be unknown.

label: Unfamiliar or technical words
why: 'Deductions' is vague and joins two things. Many people know only take-home pay, so they may report that instead.

label: Answer likely to be edited
why: Income is private; some people may skip or understate it. The shown options include no don't-know or prefer-not-to-say route. Middle options were not shown.

label: Asks two things at once
quote: to get to work and to access essential services such as healthcare
why: Two different things are asked at once. A person for whom work is easy to reach but healthcare is hard has no single true answer.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
why: Retired people, unemployed people, people working from home and others do not travel to work. No not-applicable option is offered, so they must guess or skip.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Which services count is left open. Respondents will think of different ones. 'Access' could mean distance, cost, waiting time or transport.

label: Unclear what, whose, where or when
why: Ease depends on how a person travels (car, bus, walking) and when. Respondents will judge on different bases unless the analyst fixes the travel meaning.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: The term has an open boundary. Respondents may or may not count messaging apps, video sites or forums, so they answer about different things.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: It is unclear which week is meant: the last 7 days, a typical week, or the current calendar week. Respondents will choose differently.

label: Respondent must add up
quote: how many hours per week do you spend
why: Frequent, scattered use must be added across days and platforms and turned into hours. Respondents will guess or round.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: The middle options are not shown, so exhaustiveness cannot be judged. The top category is about 3 hours a day and cuts off heavy users.

label: Asks two things at once
quote: deserve to be punished severely, even if this means longer prison sentences
why: Asks about what people deserve, how harsh punishment should be, and longer prison terms at once. A respondent may want to answer each part differently.

label: Pushes toward one answer
quote: even if this means longer prison sentences
why: The 'even if' clause treats longer sentences as an accepted cost and pushes toward agreement. 'Deserve' adds a moral push.

label: Stem states only one side
quote: People who commit serious crimes deserve to be punished severely
why: Only the harsher position is stated. The opposite position (lighter or shorter punishment) is not in the stem.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Respondents will picture different offences. 'Severely' is also vague: it could mean prison length, prison conditions or other penalties.

label: Agree-disagree instead of construct's terms
quote: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
why: Agree-disagree invites acquiescence. Options in the construct's own terms (shorter or longer sentences) would measure the view more directly.

label: No route for no opinion
quote: a scale running from Strongly agree to Strongly disagree
why: No don't-know or no-opinion option is shown. Respondents with no firm view on sentencing may have to invent an answer.

label: Asks two things at once
quote: during the day and after dark
why: Someone who feels safe by day but unsafe at night has no single true answer. The two times need separate answers.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: The edge of a neighbourhood is open. Respondents may picture their street, a few blocks or the wider district, which may change answers.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
why: Some people never go out after dark. They must imagine it or guess. Dark falls at different hours by season. Depends on what the analyst wants measured.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Respondents may think of a family doctor, a specialist, a nurse, a dentist or a pharmacist. The boundary is open, so answers refer to different things.

label: No truthful answer for non-doers
why: Someone who needed no appointment in the past 12 months has no true answer on this scale. They must skip, guess or pick a false point.

label: Hard recall or mental arithmetic
why: Respondents with several appointments or needs over a year must average mixed experiences into one rating. Recent or memorable ones may dominate.

label: Pushes toward one answer
quote: Research consistently shows that children benefit from having a parent at home in the early years.
why: States a claim as fact and appeals to research. This pushes respondents toward 'important' and gives them a reason before they form their own view.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Could mean being at home all day, not doing paid work, or working from home. Respondents will picture different arrangements.

label: Measures something other than the construct
why: The lead-in speaks of 'a parent' but the question asks only about mothers. Whether the question should cover mothers only, fathers, or either parent is the analyst's decision.

label: Words with more than one meaning
quote: the way things are going in your life
why: This idiom can mean how life is now or which direction it is heading. Respondents may answer different questions.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: Some respondents may judge their mood right now, others their life these days. The time frame has no clear boundaries.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: Only the end points are labelled, so the middle points are open to different readings. This is a defensible design choice.

label: Asks two things at once
why: A respondent may be happy with how many places exist but unhappy with the cost. One answer cannot show both.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
quote: How satisfied are you with the availability and affordability of childcare services in your area?
why: Assumes everyone has a view of childcare. People with no children or no need for it have no option to say so and may guess.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: It is unclear what counts: nurseries, childminders, after-school care, or help from relatives. Respondents may picture different things.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Respondents may take 'area' as street, town or region, so the place they judge differs.

label: Pushes toward one answer
quote: Considering the urgent need to address climate change and the fact that individual actions collectively make a significant difference
why: States contested claims as fact and pushes respondents to report changes. It also assumes they accept those claims.

label: Unfamiliar or technical words
why: A technical term. Respondents may not know what it covers, so each may picture different actions.

label: Long or stacked sentence
quote: to what extent have you made changes to your daily habits specifically to reduce your personal carbon footprint over the past year
why: A long stem with a premise clause and several qualifiers. Respondents may lose the core question.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: Start and end are not stated. Respondents may count a calendar year, 12 months, or a different span.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Unclear which habits count (energy, travel, food, shopping) and how big a change must be. Respondents will each pick their own.

label: No truthful answer for non-doers
why: People who already lived in a low-carbon way before the period cannot truthfully say they made changes, so this answer misdescribes them.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
quote: A great deal to Not at all
why: Middle options were not shown, so labelling, midpoint and balance cannot be judged. Confirm that all points are labelled and evenly spaced.

label: Answer likely to be edited
quote: individual actions collectively make a significant difference
why: This framing makes a low answer look unfavourable, so respondents who made few changes may over-report.

label: Asks two things at once
why: Voluntary work and unpaid work are different things. Unpaid work could mean a family business or an internship, so respondents may count different activities.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Unclear what counts: a church, a sports club, a school group or a charity. Respondents will draw the line in different places.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: No start or end point is given. Respondents may think of the calendar year or the last 12 months, and recall fades over that span.

label: Count or rate mismatched to recall
why: 'Times' is not defined (day, session or task). Regular volunteers cannot count each occasion over a year and must guess.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: The top category is low for regular volunteers, who may read it as the norm. The middle options were not shown, so they could not be checked.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
quote: How adequate is the amount of space
why: The stem asks about adequacy, but the options run from too much to too little. Respondents cannot tell whether 'far too much' counts as adequate.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Space could mean floor area, number of rooms, storage or outdoor areas. Respondents may each think of something different.

label: Unclear what, whose, where or when
why: Members of a household may have different needs, and respondents must decide whose needs to weigh. This depends on what the analyst wants measured.

label: Asks two things at once
quote: argue about money and about how to raise your children
why: Two topics in one question. A respondent who argues often about money but rarely about children has no single true answer.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
why: Assumes the respondent has a partner. Single respondents have no true answer, and 'partner' may be read as a business partner or a spouse only.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
why: Assumes the respondent has children to raise. Respondents without children, or with grown children, cannot answer truthfully.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
quote: How often do you and your partner argue
why: No time frame. Respondents choose their own period, such as this week or the whole relationship, so answers are not comparable.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
quote: a scale running from Very often to Never
why: 'Very often' and similar words mean different frequencies to different people. The middle options are not shown, so balance and labels could not be checked.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Could mean any disagreement or only raised voices. Respondents may set the threshold differently. The analyst may want to say what counts.

label: Pushes toward one answer
quote: Given the recent scandals in government
why: States scandals as fact and primes a negative view. Respondents may also read 'recent' and 'scandals' differently, so answers lean toward low trust.

label: Attitude object not named or bounded
quote: trust do you have in politicians
why: 'Politicians' could mean national, local, own party, or all. Respondents will each picture a different group, so answers are not comparable.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: 'Public interest' is abstract. Respondents may take it to mean the country, their area, or people like them.

label: Respondent must add up
quote: socialising, watching television, reading, or using the internet for personal enjoyment
why: Respondent must recall several different activities and add their hours in their head to give one total.

label: Long or stacked sentence
quote: not including time spent on domestic tasks, caring responsibilities, or personal grooming, but including any time spent on hobbies
why: One long sentence with stacked exclusions and inclusions is hard to hold in mind while answering.

label: Negation in the question
quote: not including time spent on domestic tasks
why: The exclusion is worded as a negation inside a long sentence, so respondents may miss it or apply it unevenly.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: The boundary is open: hobbies such as cooking or gardening may count as domestic tasks, and the internet may overlap with TV or socialising.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: 'Typical' is undefined; respondents with varying days or shifts must average in their head, and the day is not named.

label: Amount asked with vague categories
why: The top category may be too low for some people, such as retired or unemployed respondents; the middle options were not shown, so exhaustiveness could not be checked.

label: Unclear what, whose, where or when
quote: how happy would you say you are
why: No time frame is given. Some respondents may rate their mood today, others their life these days, so answers may not be comparable. Depends on the intended construct.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: Only the end points have labels, so respondents may read the middle points differently. A defensible choice; the brief gives no analysis need.

label: Attitude object not named or bounded
why: Respondents may think of parties, government, local issues or world events. A short definition would give everyone the same object in mind; the analyst decides what it covers.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: 'Quite' can mean 'fairly' or 'very', and 'hardly' is less common. Respondents may place the middle labels differently.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: No time frame or comparison standard is given. Respondents may think of today, the past year, or people their own age, and may mean body or mind.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: "Fair" may read as mildly positive or as the middle. The scale then has an uneven midpoint, which can shift answers toward the good end.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: 'Nowadays' has no clear start point. Some respondents may think of this week, others of this year, so they may judge different periods.

label: Attitude object not named or bounded
why: Respondents may think of different things: the global process, local weather, or effects on themselves. Worry about each could differ. A short definition or a narrower object may help.

label: No route for no opinion
quote: Not at all worried to Extremely worried
why: No visible route for people with no view or little knowledge. They may choose a scale point they have not really formed. Whether to add one depends on your aims.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
quote: How often do you eat fruit
why: No time frame is given. Respondents choose their own period (typical day, recent week, whole year), so answers are not comparable.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: The boundary is open. Fresh, dried, canned, fruit in cooked dishes or yoghurt, and smoothies may or may not be counted.

label: Long or stacked sentence
why: The exclusion trails after the main question and is awkward. Respondents may miss it, or be unsure whether other fruit drinks are also excluded.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
quote: a scale running from Three times or more a day to Never
why: The middle options were not shown, so they were not assessed. Check that the units stay consistent and the categories do not overlap.

label: Words with more than one meaning
quote: over your life in general nowadays
why: Respondents may think of different parts of life (work, money, health) and different time spans, since 'nowadays' has no start point.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: Only the end points are labelled, so respondents may read the nine middle points differently. A defensible design choice if comparability with other data matters.
